utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Julian Nicholls with Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning for the four of you. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours it's John Ackerman again with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic. Nice to see you this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good morning to you, the three of you. So let's proceed. Witness -- usher? Madam, the usher is going to ask you to give you the text of the solemn declaration so that you repeat it once more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpreters have a bit of a problem, the channel 7 on which we hear the witness is mutually exclusive with the channel on which we hear everything else. So if we turn on channel 7 to hear the witness, we don't hear the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what do you want us to do?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the technical people could do something so that when we listen to the witness we can also hear you and everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so much. When I was about to come in the courtroom and the Registrar told me that there were no technical problems today and no preliminaries, I said, "How come?"

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The technician is going to see what they can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, would it help if we all switch off the -- I think that's the only way we can help the interpreters, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Normally, we just allow one person to talk at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's difficult in this courtroom. You know that. So, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Nicholls will be proceeding with his examination-in-chief. Thank you. Please, as soon as you finish with your question, switch off the microphone so that we try and make the problem a little bit less cumbersome. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm now going to continue talking about the same topic we were on yesterday. Please remember again that you do not need to say your name. And I'm going to be asking you about the delegation which visited Omarska, you said around the 15th of July. First I want to go back and ask you some questions about the arrival and the greeting which you started describing yesterday by the camp commander, Meakic. Then I'll move on and ask you some questions about how the delegation moved to around the corner, which you started to indicate yesterday. Then I'll ask you about what you saw there. And you had started to describe how prisoners were singing to the delegation. Okay? So we'll do it step by step that way. And it might help if the witness could be given again 1128.4/1, which is the same diagram which we were using yesterday. And can I just ask to be careful to confirm that the voice distortion is working since we have some technical problem this morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you check?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's working quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you hear me now, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner was right, yes. We need court maintenance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] I didn't hear your question at all because I wasn't tuned in to the right channel. I would kindly ask you to repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls could I ask you to repeat your question, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I hope it's working now. Just relax. I'm going to ask you again about the same topics we went over yesterday and move through it step by step in a little bit more detail. So first I'm going to ask you about the arrival of the delegation in Omarska camp, which you said was around July 15th. The first part we'll talk about is the arrival of the delegation and the greeting by the camp commander. Then after we are done with that I'll ask you some questions about how the delegation moved around the corner and you saw them through the other part of the window, which you started to talk about yesterday. Then I'll ask you some questions about how you saw the inmates, the prisoners, singing to the delegation and you started talking about that yesterday as well. And then finally I'll ask you some questions about how the delegation left or went out of your view, out of your field of vision. Were you able to hear everything I've just said to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have no translation. No interpretation. I don't know what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Jevtovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. JEVTOVIC
utterances.text: I had translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what's happening. Perhaps one of the technicians could come in the courtroom and check things out because we are wasting precious time. I'm sorry about this, Mr. Nicholls, I know it's not your fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we have a test transmission, please? Can you hear -- can you follow in a thank that you can understand now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's all right now. I can hear the interpreters now clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, again, please, I'm sorry about this. It's the third time you're putting the question. So go ahead. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We are going to briefly go over the same topic you started talking about yesterday before we had to stop. I'm going to first ask you some questions about the arrival of the delegation at Omarska camp, which you witnessed, and you said yesterday was around July 15th. And how you saw the delegation being greeted by the camp commander Meakic. After we are done with that, I'll ask you a few questions about how you saw the delegation move and where they went to next from the spot where they were greeted. Then I'll ask you a few questions about how what you started to talk about yesterday, how you saw some inmates singing songs, you described them as a choir, for the delegation. And then finally, I'll ask you to tell the Court about how this delegation left and you couldn't see them any more. And then we'll have a few closing questions. So first, if you can look again just to catch up and confirm where we were yesterday, if you look at the exhibit in front of you, number 1 represents -- correct me if I'm wrong -- the restaurant or canteen, the position in the restaurant or canteen where you were when you first saw the delegation arrive. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Number 2 represents where you saw the camp commander greeting the delegation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you first saw this delegation somewhere around where you've marked 2 on the map, you said you saw an APC carrier. I take it there were some other vehicles. How many people -- I'm not talking about the escort but if you remember, approximately how many people were in the delegation that came to visit Omarska that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a group of people. I identified them clearly yesterday. That's Radoslav Brdjanin, Vojo Kupresanin, Radislav Vukic, Stojan Zupljanin, and Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nicholls, one moment, Mr. Nicholls. Madam, yesterday you also mentioned someone else in addition. You mentioned another name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Momir Talic. I don't know why I omitted him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I believe that yesterday you did not mention Simo Drljaca. Are you sure that he was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention him yesterday, although I'm sure he was there. I don't know why I forgot him yesterday. There may have been other people whom I did not enumerate because I'm not sure about them. I only mentioned those who I'm absolutely certain about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. So just to be clear, in addition to the people you've mentioned today and yesterday, there may have been other persons present in that delegation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was -- when this greeting was taking place at point 2 which you've marked on the diagram, were the members of the delegation who you've named facing towards you? Were you able to see them clearly at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could see them clearly. The people I mentioned were facing me, and I could see them distinctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did these persons, the people in the delegation you've mentioned, what were they doing during this greeting? Were they doing anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they heard this report, accompanied by Zeljko Meakic's salute. They stood there for a while while he greeted them, and then they started walking towards the tarmac, they turned around the corner, walked a certain distance, and stopped in front of this choir made up of inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, still staying with during -- at the spot where you saw the greeting, could you hear what was being said even though you were in the restaurant at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard the odd word but I couldn't really hear what was being said. I saw the commander raising his hand in salute, turning towards this high-ranking delegation, saluting them. I don't know exactly how long this ceremony took before the delegation walked on towards the tarmac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Had you personally -- did you know this delegation was coming that day? Did you have any advance notice? Were you told that anything special was going to happen that day? Or was it a complete surprise to you when this delegation arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we who were in the camp and working at the restaurant, we had a feeling that somebody was -- something was in the air, that something was about to happen, but we didn't know exactly what. We could hear the rehearsals of those Chetnik songs that were to be sung that day in front of the delegation. However, nobody told us expressly that a high-ranking delegation was supposed to arrive that day to the camp to visit. Later on of course, when all that was over, there was talk among the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, normally, in the restaurant or canteen which you've pointed out to us, that is somewhere where you had to work during the day. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the rule. Every day, we, the women, worked in the restaurant where the inmates of Omarska received their one meal of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: While you were watching this greeting and you'd first -- and you first saw the members of this delegation, the people you've told us about, did you have to work? Were you working at that time or were you able to watch what was going on without any distractions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could observe what was going on without any distraction because there was no work to be done at the moment, no food to be distributed. All our everyday activities at the camp had been suspended and everything was concentrated on the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you can tell me, you stated that Radoslav Brdjanin was amongst that delegation that you recognised him and that you're sure he was one of the members. Can you tell us, please, how you know that? How did you recognise Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brdjanin was a prominent public figure occupying an important political position, so I had had occasion, since the time when the nationalist-oriented parties in Bosnia had taken over, to see him frequently in the media, in the press, and the electronic media. He was a frequent guest in TV programmes and his face was very familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Prior to that, to this day in July, around mid-July, had you ever to your knowledge, had you ever seen Mr. Brdjanin in person before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had never been personally acquainted with him. I was never near the political circles in power at the time, nor I had any opportunity to meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How far away during the greeting and salute which you've told us about, approximately how far away do you think you were - if you could give an estimate - from Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been 4 or 5 metres approximately, but I was very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to be clear and be clear for the Chamber. At what point did you in your mind say, That's Radoslav Brdjanin? Was this an instant recognition? Did you realise this at some point later after the delegation had left? Did anybody talk to you and that's what made you think this was Mr. Brdjanin? Can you describe how you in your mind knew or believed this was Radoslav Brdjanin you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them clearly as soon as they stopped in front of Zeljko Meakic, and as soon as he started greeting and addressing them. I recognised him instantly, as soon as it all began. Nor did I learn it from anyone else. I saw it and heard it with my own eyes and ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you could again look at the exhibit next to you, can you just -- I don't think we need to mark it but could you just show us how the delegation moved from point 2 where they next moved to and stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, as I said, number 1 marks my position at the canteen in the restaurant, number 2 is the position of Zeljko Meakic the camp commander who was saluting the delegation. And the spot where the delegation remained for a while before moving on, around the corner, towards the pista, the tarmac, and stopped in front of this choir here that was standing on the tarmac. So this is the path along which they walked, the route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If the witness could be given a pen I think it would be helpful if she marked where the people she saw lining up, the choir, as she calls them, were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So if you could just draw a line, please, marking where so that we can see how the prisoners were lined up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ask her to put a 4 against that line, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you please mark that line with a 4 at one end of the line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could now show the witness, this was Exhibit P1128.5. I'll give her a clean copy in case Your Honours want it to be marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you take a moment to look at that, please, Witness, is that from the part of it you can see, that's another photo of a model of Omarska camp, is that also a fair and accurate representation of part of the camp as it was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you, without marking it, can you point to the spot, if it's on there, where you were during this time of the delegation. First where you were, if it's visible there, when you were able to see the greeting which you've talked about? In other words, where would point number 1 be on this diagram, which you'd marked on the earlier diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is clearly visible, very much so, and I will show you on this photograph or rather on this model, because that part of the restaurant can be easily seen. I was here, this corner, then the delegation is moving in this direction, and now I'm here in this part.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please speak towards the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you please arrange -- yeah, move the microphone a little bit so that when the witness is looking at the ELMO, she can be heard? It's not your problem. We are fixing that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Then just to be clear, this corner which you're now pointing at represents the area where you were the entire time? You've moved within that glassed area to see the delegation first while they were greeted and then while they were watching the prisoners who were lined up singing. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite right. As a rule, we were sitting in this corner here, which I've just pointed at. The last one. There was a table, perhaps two or three chairs, and a radiator and that is where we sat at the time when we were not working somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could this be exhibited as a -- that's all right. Sorry, it's already in. And maybe could the other diagram be put back on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to, if you could, just describe the scene as you remember it, of the prisoners singing for the delegation. If you could describe how that started? You started to yesterday. What types of songs they were singing and if you can, how many prisoners approximately there were at that time, lined up, where you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, what I said yesterday, I will repeat that. So I am standing here. I was right here in this corner, in this part, marked here on this drawing, number 1, and this high-ranking delegation arrives. I see an APC nearby and clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At this point, I think that's clear. I'm just asking about what you saw at the time that the prisoners were singing to the delegation. How long -- let me ask you this: How long did that singing continue? How many songs were these prisoners forced to sing, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just said it seems to me, although it was -- it is very difficult to pinpoint the time, but it could have been 10, 15 minutes, during which nationalistic, chauvinistic Chetnik songs were sung, "od Topole pa do Raume gore, Svud su straze djemerala Draze, Ko to kaze Ko to laze," "Who is saying, who is lying?" There were various salutes with three raised fingers, they cry out, "Long live Serbia, long live Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you were able to see, could you tell what the reaction of Mr. Brdjanin and the other members of the delegation was to this display?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they listened attentively to the salutes and the singing went on. They were standing in front of that choir, and I thought that they were addressing them, that one member of the delegation was addressing the choir. But it was really very loud, because they were -- the singing was going on, the shouts were going on, so that one could not really hear what the members of the delegation were saying to the inmates standing in the choir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think you've been clear but just to be sure, were you able to also see Mr. Brdjanin at this point during the singing which you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Now they are facing -- at some point they had their backs on me because they were looking at the choir, from the place where I was, I could now see only their backs, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What type of clothing was Mr. Brdjanin wearing? Was he wearing any kind of uniform or was he in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the clothes were civilian but I can't really remember. I can't remember what those civilian clothes looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, briefly you stated that you recognised Mr. Brdjanin from seeing him in the media, on TV and in newspapers and in magazines. Did you personally know any of the members of that delegation? In other words, were there any that you recognised from having known them rather than just from having seen their pictures before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Simo Drljaca, the then chief of the public security centre in Prijedor, and I also knew Stojan Zupljanin because we had been at the university together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When you first saw this delegation, did you have any -- how did it make you feel? What did you think they were there for? Did you have any ideas, any -- did it trigger anything in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I didn't know. First I thought that the delegation would come to the restaurant where the women were so that they could see us there. I did not know the reason for the visit, and perhaps I was hoping against hope that they would sympathise with us and perhaps do something to alleviate our position in the camp and perhaps do something about our release from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how did you feel when you saw these prisoners singing songs for the delegation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very painful scene. People exhausted by torture, with the conditions in the camp, who had lost weight significantly. My impression was it was a choir of skeletons singing. I couldn't understand where they drew their strength from to be able to sing so loudly and shout out those war cries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did the delegation ever come into the restaurant or did you in any other way personally meet the members of the delegation face to face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The delegation did not enter the restaurant. No. While I was there, nobody did, and I did not meet any of the members of the delegation. I mean, I didn't have any particular meeting with any one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown, this is P1547/S238? It's also marked as -- this is a Kozarski Vjesnik article headlined, either, "It's difficult or it's tough for everyone," depending on the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, if you could ask you to take a moment, it's quite a short article dated 17th July, 1992. If your copy is clear enough, could you please read that to yourself and just tell me when you're done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This article dated 17th July, 1992, in paragraph 2, refers to Krajina representatives Radoslav Brdjanin, Radislav Vukic, Predrag Radic and Stojan Zupljanin, and then the next paragraph states, "After they visited the areas where combat operations had taken place and collection centres, the guests from the Krajina thanked their hosts for their hospitality and their efforts put into creating a new Serbian state at this area. At the decisive moment when Alija Izetbegovic already thought he had turned Prijedor into a new Alcatraz," and then it quotes Radoslav Brdjanin as talking about the situation in Prijedor being a job well done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the usher please move the text down so the interpreters can see it, since we cannot hear Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is dated 17th July, 1992, talking about a visit to collection centres a day earlier. Could that have been the same visit which you've been discussing in your mind? Do you believe that's the same visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, she could have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite sure about that and this corroborates what I told you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't jump like that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She was in the middle of an answer and you didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- let her finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There could just be no basis for her to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you should have waited until I gave you the go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's your objection, Mr. Ackerman? Because I couldn't hear the two of you talk -- speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is: After reading the article, could that have been the same visit you've been discussing, in your mind? Do you believe that's the same visit? My objection is she would have absolutely no basis to answer that question. How could she possibly know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you can rephrase your question, Mr. Nicholls, by asking the witness whether the visit to the camp by the delegation that she referred to earlier coincided according to her, as far as the date is concerned? In other words, with the visit that is mentioned in the document that has been just shown to her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to clear up that the visit could have been coincided with, as His Honour stated, what's laid out in this article taking place on the 16th of July. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did coincide, as the Presiding Judge has said. It coincides with my story about the delegation's visit, and this article corroborates it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to a different topic and I think we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into closed session for a while, Madam Registrar, please. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think private session is sufficient, isn't it? I don't think we have to close all these things here. Private session gets us the same place just without closing all those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it, Madam Registrar? Would that be okay with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to discuss with you that time in July when you claim that Mr. Brdjanin visited Omarska. The first thing -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to go back into private session for just a moment. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back into private session for a moment. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, the people you claim to have seen during this, what you call delegation visit to Omarska, were Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Zupljanin, Dr. Vukic, Simo Drljaca, Momir Talic, Vojo Kupresanin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you be any more specific about the date that you claim it was when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said around the 15th. It could have been a day before or a day after. I already said it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you believe that this article you saw from Kozarski Vjesnik this morning dated the 17th may very well have been connected to that meeting, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. It so happened, whether by accident or -- but be that as it may, it tallies with what I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just going back to that article for just a second, I think you'll recall that your attention was brought to a part of that article which purports to quote Mr. Brdjanin that, "The situation in Prijedor is an example of a job well done, and it's a pity that many people in Banja Luka are not yet aware of it." Of course, you of your own personal knowledge have no idea whether Mr. Brdjanin actually said such a thing or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned it from that article. It was from that article that I learned what he had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is the same newspaper that you told us just a moment ago was an unreliable pack of lies, basically, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes, the Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. You left the camp, didn't you, on, I think, the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You told us during your examination by Mr. Nicholls today, page 14, line 22, that when you saw that delegation there, you were hoping that they would do something about our release from there. That was one of your reactions to seeing them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. The mood changed and reactions also changed. At some point, I thought that perhaps it might help us to get out of the camp, however, I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And how long at that time had you been there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the 9th until the 15th, 16th, or the 17th. From the 9th of June, 1992, so there you are, 20, 21 days, and 15 there, so it was well over a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it's the case, isn't it, that just two weeks after this delegation had come that you were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was released on the 3rd of August, 1992, so it was sometime after the visit. And we were not released, we were transferred to another camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then rather immediately released from there, weren't you? I think you were there five days, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember whether or not you saw Predrag Radic in this group that you claim visited Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not really spot him, and I don't want to speak about things that I'm not sure about. I said that in addition to those individuals whose names I gave you today and yesterday, there were some others, but I simply did not -- did not spot them exactly, did not identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You told us today that, with regard to Mr. Brdjanin, that you -- you knew who he was when you saw him there, when you claim to have seen him there, because he occupied an important political position. What political position did you understand that he occupied in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for the record, that wasn't her exact answer. She said she'd seen him. She knew who he was. Because he had that position, he was in the media a lot, and she had seen him on television and papers, not just because he had this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your honour, I wasn't limiting her. She said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She definitely referred to Brdjanin as an important political figure who held an important position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I suggest we don't lose or waste time. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman, because I do remember it very vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What important political position was it that you claim that he occupied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ranked very highly in the Serb Democratic Party. He was the President of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and the president of the Krajina Crisis Staff. I learned that from the media, as I have already said. There was frequent talk about that on television, on radio, or the written press. His photographs also appeared, because he was frequently in various television programmes. That is how I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two questions now that I need to go back to private session, and then I think we will be finished with private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to private session for a while. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman referred you to P1547 -- I think it's /S238. That is the Kozarski Vjesnik article 17 July, 1992, and questioned you about whether this paper printed lies and about how you would know whether or not the statement made was actually made by Radoslav Brdjanin. You testified that you heard him in the media and on the news very often before you were in Omarska. Did you listen carefully to the statements he made in those -- before you were in Omarska that you heard made in magazines and on television or radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this article, which purports to quote Radoslav Brdjanin, it states, "After saying that the situation in Prijedor is an example of a job well done and that it is a pity that many people in Banja Luka are not yet aware of it," he also states, "these Muslims had fled the neighbouring municipalities and already making plans to heed the call of Jihad." Is that the same as the type of statements you used to hear him make before you were put in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Verbal threats, accusations, torture, which is even worse. The staff of the camp used to tell us that we were there because it was our fault, that we were guilty of waging this holy war, Jihad, that we were guilty for having voted for Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear for the record, where you say, "Yes, yes. Verbal threats, accusations," et cetera, are you talking there about statements you heard Brdjanin make in the media? Or are you talking about what you heard in the camp? Because you've put those together in that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The message was the same, filled with hatred, nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Janu will be asking you a question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Madam, Mr. Ackerman in his cross-examination took you to the point where you visited your flat, the new lady was there and you said she offered you a coffee. And he asked you if you asked her for something what was dear to you. My question is this: Did she offer you that you can take something, what is dear to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She didn't offer me anything. She said that she liked the apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a final question arising out of the question that has been put to you by Judge Janu. Why on earth did you decide to accept to go inside what was previously your own flat and have a coffee with a person that had taken possession of it and also of all your belongings? What were you trying to prove or achieve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT1 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she had invited me. She was pretty nice, and I accepted. Perhaps at that moment, I was naive thinking that she might return the apartment to me. Because after leaving the camp, I had no idea where to go, where I could spend the night, where I would live, until I was finally put up by my own friends and acquaintances. She even asked me why I was so anxious, nervous. I told her that I had this strange sensation, as if I were not sitting in my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That brings us to the end of your testimony in this trial. I do understand that this must -- this wasn't an easy time for you, to come here and give evidence on certain events that you allege have taken place in your life. On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence, and I can put your mind at rest that you will receive all the assistance that you require now to enable you to return to your place of residence. I thank you once more and the usher will accompany you out of the courtroom. One moment. While she goes out -- yes, exactly. I think we ought to pull down the curtains for a while. We don't need to go into closed session? No. Or do we?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think it's you, Madam Richterova, who is taking over now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, it's me. And the following witness was granted image distortion, so we can as well use -- take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we leave the curtains down for the time being. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, are you just going back to your place? Do we need to go into some kind of private session while he walks in or whatever, Madam Chuqing? No. Just -- At this point in time, if you are taking an hour, and Mr. Brdjanin -- Mr. Ackerman is taking half an hour, I don't see any point in bringing the other witness, because it would have been okay had we finished with the previous witness 20 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah. This one was sent back, so we will finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Ms. Sutherland, can I rely on you to liaise with Ms. Korner and take a decision? We are here. If you want to bring in the witness even for five minutes, we are prepared to hear him but it's up to you any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you give me one second to set up things before we start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. In the meantime, I'll handle the witness. He's got a pseudonym, correct? Pseudonym and image distortion? Is that right? Yes. Let me check it once more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the witness enjoys voice distortion -- image distortion and pseudonym, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. He was granted a pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- on behalf of the Tribunal, I welcome you. You are about to start giving evidence, and before you do so, our rules require from you that you enter -- you make, a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is in the hands of the usher who has just handed it over to you. Please read it out loud and that's your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's going to happen very briefly is the following: You won't be here for a long time. First, for about an hour or so, you're going to be asked questions by Madam Richterova for the Prosecution. I suppose you are already familiar with her. You know who she is. And she will then be followed by, I would imagine, Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for the accused Radoslav Brdjanin. Madam Richterova, the witness is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At first I have to apologise to the witness for the delay we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, that piece of paper supposedly contains your name and surname. Please don't read it. Just have a look at it and if it contains your name and surname, just say yes. And then we have a look at it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, please show it to the Defence and to us. The reason for all this -- these precautions, sir, is to protect you. We have placed an order for some protective measures. You will not be referred to by your name in this courtroom but only by a nom de plume that we have given to you, and in addition, no one can see your face because we have agreed to protect you in another manner, also by image distortion. If in fact you press the button video on your monitor, when you are talking, you will see how others will be seeing you. And that's by way of protecting your identity as you actually yourself requested. Thank you. Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This piece of paper will be Prosecution Exhibit under seal P1620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it will be under seal, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go to the private session just for a moment for the background information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are in open session. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, contrary to what Your Honours had basically ordered much earlier in the case, just at this very moment was I advised that exhibits are going to be used with this witness, what those exhibits are going to be, and this is just a violation of everything that we have been trying to do in this case, and I object very strongly to it. The Prosecution knows that I have an e-mail address that I watch constantly. They could have easily sent this to me yesterday evening. They probably could have handed it to me yesterday afternoon. I'm sure it was known then. But to -- at the very beginning of a witness who I have already said that I would finish rather quickly, to hand this material to me, I think, is unfair and violates your prior orders. And all I want to say about it is I may need to ask you to allow me to delay my cross-examination until tomorrow, at least part of it, but I will look through these documents as quickly as I can now. I may not need to ask for that but I just think it's not fair to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I prepared the list of exhibits on Thursday and as I was informed by Ms. Gustin, she handed over this list to the Defence. So I really do not know whether a gremlin took it from the locker or -- but it was handed over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We got it now but what I -- what I see here is, Chuqing, for Judges, SLO, you, and J. Ackerman. This is what's written on this yellow slip, which is different from the list obviously because these are the documents, not the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I apologise what happened. I received this information and I tried to hand over this as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman? Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Ms. Gustin believes that she handed this to me at some time -- sometime this week, I cannot -- I will not stand here and say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last week, she said, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will not stand here and say 100 per cent that I never received it. I just can't do that because she is reliable. I don't recall ever seeing it. I don't think I ever saw it, but in any event we can go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any way, I think point taken, Mr. Ackerman, also Madam Richterova. I think Mr. Ackerman has been fair to leave open the possibility of being able to proceed and conclude today. However, if he does find a difficulty, then obviously, we have to protect the interests of the accused here as well, and we will have to postpone the cross-examination until it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, can you briefly describe the life in your village before the war in Croatia started, and after the war started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Well, I can say that we -- I mean, all peoples had good relations and got along well. We were all together, but when the war in Croatia started, then the change towards us -- the Croats changed. We all of a sudden became a different people and they started insulting us and treating us differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I want to focus on the year 1992. Was there any restriction on movement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: That's right. The movement was restricted. Tomasica and on its boundary, there were guards. So that we, the Croats, from Tomasica could not go to Sasina. And they had guards every 100 or 200 metres. We could move around Tomasica. We could even reach the shops, but we could not get out, because Serb troops came from other places, unknown, and under arms, so that we dared not move further away from Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said you could reach the shops. Did you go shopping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No. I didn't, because I was afraid. There were many troops from other villages and they were drinking a lot, and we didn't know them and this is why I was afraid to go shopping. But they did not prohibit us from selling goods except that we were ashamed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the year 1992, was there any announcement to hand over weapons, legally or illegally obtained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: 1992. I don't know which month, but there was a statement in Prijedor, through Sanski Most, that those who owned weapons should return them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said a statement. Did you hear this statement and was it on television or on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I heard it on the radio. When they said it, I didn't have a TV set. I still do not have one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember exactly what was said with respect to surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I remember they said they -- that people should return weapons to the Prijedor police and Sanski Most police. That is what I remember. I know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you own a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether anybody else returned or handed over the weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: In Tomasica, there were three men who had pistols and licensed pistols, and they came and seized their weapons. I know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the period of 1992, are you aware that there would be searches, that there would be searches of houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in 1992, did you see coming soldiers to your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I started to visit a neighbour. It was the 10th of July, 1992, and I saw soldiers at Tomo Grgic's house. The house was surrounded. They asked me where I was headed. I told them. They said, "Go home. Today the houses are searched." And I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So on this occasion, was the houses searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was your house searched that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did the soldiers find any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Not at my place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When we are talking about these soldiers, do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I know one, Slavko Torbica from Rakelici. I didn't know him until then; I met him on that occasion. And I knew a Croat, Andjelko Kaurin, who volunteered to join the Serb army, and he searched Croat houses together with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember what these soldiers wear? Did they wear normal uniforms or camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: They wore normal uniforms. The soldiers I do not know them, I only know Slavko Torbica from Rakelici and Andjelko Kaurin. I don't know those other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On this occasion, was anybody arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: On that occasion, they arrested Juro Grgic, Tomo, and Vinko Topalovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know where these people were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Those people were taken in a van to Andjelko Kaurin's house. A lamb was being roasted there and drinking was going on, and then they took people towards Prijedor. In which direction from there, I don't know. Andjelko Kaurin might know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Have you seen these three people ever since?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, I want now you to focus on the events which occurred in December 1992, but before we start, did anything else happen in your village between July and December 1992 which would struck your attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yeah. In November 1992 - I don't know the date, the exact date Ivo Toplovic was killed, taken out from the house, taken 50 metres away, and the next day his body was found by people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who killed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I will focus on the events which occurred in December 1992. On 2nd of December, you were tasked to cut wood. Who gave you this order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: On the 2nd of December, 1992, Bore Stojic came with another Serb soldier. The place of Busnovi, they came to Tomasica, to Andjo Maric's house, and ordered us, the Croats, to go to the boundary between Sasina and Tomasica in three days' time to get out 150 cubic metres of firewood. Some people started to protest a little, Bore Stojic replied, "Don't you make me come to get you the second time."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, who was Bore Stojic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Why, he was dressed as a soldier. I don't know anything else -- oh, yes, he had a rifle too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: As a -- you said he was dressed as a soldier. Do you know which army he belonged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you cut the wood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It means until the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the 5th of December is the day when the event occurred. Can you describe what happened that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So please tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, as we were driving the timber, Mile Topalovic and I stayed back in the woods and Juro Sedic, Mato Sedic. And the timber was driven away by Pero Topalovic, Pero Popovic, Mile Komljenovic, Ante Komljenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that these people took the woods away. Where was this wood taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: It was taken to Franjo Salic's house, as Bore Stojic had ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the people you just listed, did they stay in that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where did they go from this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: They went back to the woods, and we, that is Mile Topalovic and I, went out of the woods, and there we met Bore Stojic. And we asked him if we could go home. And Bore said, "Sure. But don't speak to anyone."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you and Mile Topalovic, where were you going? Did you go home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: We started for our homes, towards Franjo Salic's house. We were some 500 metres away still, and we heard some shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After you heard these shots, what was your reaction? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Well, we did not really have any foreboding that something would happen because Serbs were always armed, and fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see -- what did you see after these shots?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: We moved forward, where some 200 metres away from Franjo Salic's house, Mile Topalovic said, "Somebody might kill us." We moved forward, and were about 100 metres away from Franjo Salic's yard. We had Marinko Topalovic, Mile Topalovic's son, with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when you reach the house or better say you said you were about 100 metres from that house, did -- what did you see went on before the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: When we fetched up at Franjo Salic's yard, five soldiers came out of Franjo's yard, and one soldier said to us, "Come on, move on, faster. What are you waiting for?" When we reached them, two soldiers started towards us, and one of them asked Mile what his name was. And Mile said, "We are bringing in the timber." And he said, "I'm not asking you what are you doing but what your name is." Mile said, "Topalovic." Then he asked me, and I answered. He asked me, "And whose is this kid?" And I said, "Mile's." The second soldier had his rifle aimed at me, at the left shoulder. The first soldier, the one who asked questions of Mile, who asked Mile what was his name, hit him with the rifle, to turn back in the direction from which we had come, and then fired a bullet in his neck.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After he fired this bullet in Mile Topalovic's head, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Mile fell, head down, swallowed something, and stayed like that. And then that first soldier ordered the second soldier, the one who had his rifle against my left shoulder, he said to him, "Well, hit, what are you waiting for?" And this second soldier hit me with a fist in the left side of my face so that I would turn back like Mile, and he fired a bullet in my left shoulder. I made one step forward and fell next to Mile. When I fell, then one of them, I don't know which one, fired a second bullet which went through my right shoulder, but I was still conscious. Marinko Topalovic was crying with pain and said, "Don't kill me. I've done nothing wrong." At that, the first soldier who had killed Mile Topalovic came up to me and fired a bullet beneath my left eye. And then I fainted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you here for a moment. You -- and I will start from the moment you were close to Franjo Salic's house. You said you saw five soldiers. Did you recognise any of these soldiers as persons you knew from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Multi-coloured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you mean a multi-coloured, does it mean a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Why, all the soldiers wore that. What else to call it? Just as I've said, of many colours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did they wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: That first soldier had a PAP, and those others, I don't know, because we had our heads down and we could not look up at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And last question about these soldiers: Did you see any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And another question is: How old approximately was Marinko Topalovic at that time, at the moment, when his father, Mile Topalovic, was shot in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I interrupted you at the moment when you said that you were shot by one of these soldiers below your eye and you lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When, what time approximately, this happened? What time of the day this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: It was around 1400, 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you came around, was it still light?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were you able to see? What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: When I came to, I sat up. I see Mile Topalovic dead, and my both left and right arms were between my legs. My right jaw was broken and my teeth were hanging down around my right leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. After you came around, did anybody come to the place where you both were lying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: When I came to, somebody let Bore Stojic know in the woods, what happened to us. Bore turned up and then Knezevic, with a car, in a Zastava. And when Bore saw us, he was taken aback but he could not pass by, because of us, because Mile was dead and I was alive. And then Renato Knezevic got out of the car and moved my legs to a side and that is how they went on. Where they went, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did these two men provide you with any help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After they left, did anybody else appear there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Later on, Goran Savic turned up in a uniform and with a rifle, and Radenko Jovic, likewise, and Nevenka Savic. Goran Savic asked me, "Neighbour, who did this to you?" I couldn't answer anything. Nevenka Savic got the cart which belonged to Pero Popovic and took me to her home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, did you say took me to her home [as interpreted]? Does it mean that she took you to her --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No. The horse cart or ox cart.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because it was on the transcript. You just named these three people. Who were they? Were they Croat? Muslims? Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they provide you with any help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After they left, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I tried to stand up. I tried to -- I put my back against the wall and with my feet on the ground, and I managed to stand up, and I started towards Ivica's house. And in Salic's yard, I saw Pero Topalovic killed, Dragica Salic killed, and Mara Salic killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you saw these three people in the yard and you said they were killed, did you see any wounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did you know that they were killed? Or I will -- excuse me, I will rephrase: How did you know that they were dead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I knew, whereas I saw Pero was on his back, Dragica Salic also on her back, and Mara Salic on her side but I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you go closer to them to be able to see what exactly happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No. I could not do it, since I was at risk too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is the time for the break. Is it possible that we would ask for a shorter break to be sure that this witness will -- of course it will depend on Mr. Ackerman, that he finishes today? Because he has been here for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, unless the Prosecutor is going much longer than they had originally planned, there is no reason we can't finish with him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we say 15 minutes' break? Is that okay with you, Mr. Ackerman? All right. Okay. 15 minutes' break. Usher and Madam Registrar, please, if the witness is leaving the courtroom, since we have image distortion, we need to take precautions so that while he's going out, he is not seen by the members of the public or is not taken on camera. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I've, had a chance to go through the documents and I'll not be asking for any additional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I had looked through them as well. I don't think they are that vitally important except to prove maybe one thing. That's all. Okay. We'll have a break of 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Richterova, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, before we adjourned, you described that you went inside of the yard of the Franjo Salic's house, and you found bodies of Pero Topalovic, Dragica Salic, and Mara Salic, and they were lying on the ground. Where did you go from, from the house of the Franjo Salic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Then I went to Ivo Knezevic's home, where Mile Causic from Ratinsko, Banja Luka, was. There was Radko Kaurin from Tomasica. There was Zeljko Jovic and Radenko Jovic, all with rifles. Mile Causic ripped his shirt and bandaged his right jaw. He said to Zeljko that I was not in life danger. At that moment, a car arrived. Zeljko Jovic went out to meet the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you for a second. You just named people who were in Ivo Knezevic's home, and you said they all had rifles. Who were these people? What ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Zeljko Jovic and Radenko Jovic had rifles. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And only these two people had their rifles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the other people you named, who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Mile Causic and the other one, Ranko Kaurin, were Croats. It was a place where pigs were slaughtered. They were in the process of slaughtering pigs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you said that Mile Causic ripped his shirt and bandaged his -- I'm sorry, your jaw. Was it the first opportunity or was it for the first time when you received any kind of help since you -- since you were shot in the woods -- I'm sorry, since you were shot in front of the house of Franjo Salic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After you were provided with this first aid, what happened then? Were you taken to a hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Dusko Kljajic put me in his car, drove me to the mine in Tomasica, where an ambulance was waiting for me. There were about 30 policemen, Serb policemen, there under arms. Slavko Torbica from Rakelici took me there, and another Serb, whose name I don't know. They took me over at that spot and they asked me whether I was a Croat. Somebody answered for me that I was, and they put me in the first available ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And with this ambulance, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: They took me to the hospital in Prijedor, where I was given an injection to calm me down, but it didn't really help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You just said that in Prijedor hospital, you got this injection. Did they provide any other help?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No. They only gave me another ambulance to be driven on to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So from Prijedor, you were transferred to Banja Luka. Which hospital in Banja Luka were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: The hospital in Banja Luka was Paprikovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This hospital, Paprikovac, was it the first hospital you were taken in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No. It was the third hospital in Banja Luka to which I was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened in the two hospitals -- you said this was the third. It means that there were two other hospitals. What happened in these two hospitals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I was taken to two hospitals where I wasn't admitted, for a reason I ignore, before I was taken to Paprikovac where I was eventually admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the transcript, it says for a reason I ignore. What do you mean by this? Were you given a reason why they didn't admit you to these two hospitals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While in the hospital in Paprikovac, what kind of help were you provided with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: When I arrived at the hospital, it was already dark. I saw a lot of knives on a table, and I understood that the doctors were saying they were going to pull out my tongue from my throat to avoid suffocation. They did that and they gave me a sedative, after which I fell asleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you woke up, what were you able to observe on your body? What did you [as interpreted] do to you with respect to treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: When I came to, I had so-called fixators on both sides of my face. I had a tube in my throat. Under my throat, I had another device to facilitate breathing. The right side of my jaw was bandaged and my mouth was bound, tied, with ordinary wire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I was admitted on the 5th of December, and discharged on the 18th January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While in the hospital, were you washed? Was your facial hair shaved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: For a long time, I went without washing or shaving. I don't know exactly for how long, because I had long spells of unconsciousness. When Drago Jovic and Vucin Jovic came from Tomasica, however, they fetched the doctor. And I don't know what they told the doctor, but after their visit, I got two blood transfusions, two full bottles of blood for transfusion and I was washed and shaved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned a second ago that you weren't washed and shaved. What were the consequences of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: The consequences were I don't know how to put it, I was covered with lice, large lice, and that itched and ached, but I couldn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So can you -- are you able to tell us approximately after how many days in the hospital you were shaved and washed for the first time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: For about 25 days, until Drago and Vucin Jovic came to visit me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it was also for the first time you receive the blood transfusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I received the drips in my legs whenever I came to. I couldn't be given drips in my arms because my arms were too heavily injured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While your mouth was tied with wire and you said that it was just an ordinary wire, were you able to receive any food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So how were you receiving food or -- what --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: I only got this drip that was inserted in my leg, but I couldn't get any nutrition through my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After they removed the wire and you received normal food for the first time, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: When the wire was removed, I was given some mashed food. However, it all came back up through my nose. When the doctor came to see me the second time, I showed him with my hands that I can't eat because the food is coming back up through my nose. And the doctor answered that a bullet had passed below my eye, through my nose, and that the injury was very serious and that's when I got real scared.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were they able to treat you properly in this hospital in Banja Luka? Or did you need -- or were you told that you need some special treatment in some other hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes. They tried their best, the physicians, to care for me, to give me proper care, but they did not have the wherewithal to treat me properly. They asked for permission to transfer me to Belgrade, but the management or whoever was supposed to sign this request refused.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While in the hospital, how would you describe the nurses? And I mean how did they treat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: The nurses were very kind and very good. One of them, nurse Slavica told the doctor every day that I need to be sent on somewhere. I don't know exactly what she meant by that but the doctor said something to shut her up. And she stopped saying eventually that I should be thrown out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I will return to my previous question about the washing. You said that you were washed for the first time after the 25th day. Then you were washed. And how did it look after that? Were you washed regularly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: For a long time after that, I wasn't washed again, and then a Muslim woman Hasnija Klipic, came to visit me in the hospital. She asked if my father was coming to visit me. I told her that I had no father. Then she asked the doctor to release me from the hospital, saying that she would take me to her home. And that's what happened. And from then on, she cared for me, washed me, and fed me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And, Witness, is it correct that after you were released from the hospital and after you spent some time with this woman, you managed to leave for a third country in which you received another medical treatment? You underwent surgeries; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT31
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you some documents which I know you didn't see before, until -- until I show you these documents. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if there is an useful purpose for showing documents to the witness that he's never seen. If the only purpose is to get them admitted, I have no objection to their admission. They can simply be marked and admitted and they stand for what they stand for. I don't know how the witness could either add or detract from them since he's not seen them before. So if that's the purpose, I have no objection and we can save a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
